result: The authors obtained crystal structures of SpNOX full-length (F397W mutant at 3.6 Å resolution) and dehydrogenase domain constructs (WT at 2.5 Å and F397W at 1.94 Å resolution), providing the first complete prokaryotic NOX structure with both transmembrane and dehydrogenase domains.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly praised the structural work. Reviewer 1 stated 'the structure of the S. pneumoniae Nox protein is an important step forward' and 'the characterization and interpretation are convincing.' Reviewer 2 noted 'the crystallography must be appreciated given the difficulty of obtaining good enzyme preparations and the flexibility of the protein' and called it 'very solid work.' Reviewer 3 emphasized 'the effort put into preparing a pure and functionally active SpNOX preparation' and the detailed description of purification and optimization.

result: The authors optimized buffer conditions for SpNOXDH stability and activity, finding that thermostability improves with increasing NaCl and glycerol but activity decreases, with optimal conditions at 300 mM NaCl and 5% glycerol at pH 6.5.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically commended 'the effort put into preparing a pure and functionally active SpNOX preparation' and noted that 'the purification and optimization of its thermostability and activity are described in detail, involving salt concentration, glycerol concentration, and pH.' This detailed optimization work was viewed positively by reviewers as supporting the quality of subsequent structural and functional studies.

result: The isolated DH domain acts as a flavin reductase, requiring supplemental FAD for activity, producing both superoxide (40% of cytochrome c reduction, SOD-sensitive) and directly reducing cytochrome c (60%, SOD-insensitive), with the flavin behaving as a co-substrate rather than a prosthetic group.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated 'the protein chemistry and biochemical analysis are well executed and carefully described,' indicating acceptance of the functional characterization of the DH domain. The reviewers did not raise concerns about the flavin reductase activity or the interpretation of SOD-sensitive vs. SOD-insensitive cytochrome c reduction.

result: Both SpNOX full-length and DH domain constructs use either NADPH or NADH as substrate with similar affinity (Km values), showing no significant discrimination between the two, which differs from eukaryotic NOX that strongly prefer NADPH.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted that 'the manuscript further carefully studies the enzyme's kinetics and substrate-specificity properties,' indicating acceptance of the substrate specificity findings. The lack of discrimination between NADPH and NADH was not questioned by reviewers.

result: Hydride transfer from NAD(P)H to FAD is the rate-limiting step in electron transfer, as evidenced by similar kcat values for full-length and DH-only constructs, indicating that the presence or absence of hemes has little effect on the rate.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated 'the manuscript nicely shows that the domain rotations are unlikely to be the main mechanistic element of NOX regulation. It rather appears that the NADPH-binding conformation is pivotal to enzyme activation.' This directly supports the authors' conclusion about hydride transfer being rate-limiting and the importance of NADPH positioning rather than domain movements.

result: F397 is critical for nicotinamide access to the flavin isoalloxazine ring, with the F397W mutation preventing activity by blocking hydride transfer through tight stacking with FAD, while F397S enhances activity by providing more space for substrate access, similar to the mechanism in FNR family domains.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 praised the work, stating 'the protein chemistry and biochemical analysis are well executed and carefully described.' The functional characterization of F397 mutants and their structural interpretation were not questioned. The reviewers accepted the mechanistic insights about F397's role in controlling substrate access and hydride transfer.

result: Flavin binding has contributions from both DH and TM domains, with the isolated DH domain showing no selectivity for flavin type (constant ~10 μM Km for all flavins) while full-length SpNOX displays 263-fold higher affinity for FAD (nM level) than lumiflavin, indicating significant interactions between FAD and the TM domain, particularly through the D-loop region.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted 'the manuscript further carefully studies the enzyme's kinetics and substrate-specificity properties,' which encompasses the flavin binding studies. The differential flavin binding between DH-only and full-length constructs was not challenged by reviewers and supports the structural interpretation of shared binding sites.

result: The SpNOXDH structure reveals a typical FNR superfamily fold with FAD-binding and NADPH-binding domains, with the isoalloxazine ring sandwiched between P234/F235 and F397. In WT, F397 imperfectly occupies the re-face position (5.3 Å distance, 40° angle), while F397W makes tight parallel stacking (3.5 Å), explaining the drastic activity differences between mutants.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated 'the crystallography must be appreciated given the difficulty of obtaining good enzyme preparations and the flexibility of the protein. Even if solved at medium resolution, the crystal structure of the full-length protein conveys relevant information.' The structural details of the DH domain and the positioning of F397 were accepted without challenge.

result: The full-length SpNOX structure shows the TM domain with 6 transmembrane helices chelating two hemes (coordinated by histidine pairs, with metal-to-metal distance ~21.5 Å), and reveals that the adenine extremity of FAD is packed in a pocket involving F399 from the DH domain and residues from the D-loop of the TM domain (particularly Y122 and R126), with R126A mutation reducing FAD affinity 23-fold.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted 'even if solved at medium resolution, the crystal structure of the full-length protein conveys relevant information,' indicating acceptance of the structural findings despite resolution limitations. The mutagenesis data supporting the role of D-loop residues in FAD binding was not questioned.

result: Structural comparison suggests that distal heme accessibility may influence the final electron acceptor, with some FRDs (MsrQ, SpNOX, CsNOX) exhibiting small extracellular loops and free access to the distal heme, while others (NOX2, DUOX) have long loops or extracellular domains creating a cap that limits access and may enforce O2 selectivity.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated 'the paper extensively refers to the previous literature and analyses the structures comprehensively with a comparison to previously reported structures of eukaryotic and prokaryotic NOXs.' The structural comparisons regarding heme accessibility were accepted as part of the comprehensive analysis.

result: The relative position of DH and TM domains does not necessarily correlate with activity. SpNOX's domain orientation is intermediate between inactive NOX2 and active DUOX1, yet SpNOX is constitutively active. The distances between FAD and heme (7.2-10.2 Å) remain compatible with electron transfer in all structures, and there is no evident correlation between DH motion and distance contraction, suggesting that domain orientation may be isoform-specific rather than representing activation states.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly stated 'the manuscript nicely shows that the domain rotations are unlikely to be the main mechanistic element of NOX regulation,' directly supporting the authors' conclusion that relative domain position does not correlate with activity. This was identified as a key contribution of the work.

result: The activated state of eukaryotic NOX requires a specific relative motion of the NBD toward the FBD to achieve productive topology in the DH domain. In SpNOX, the distance between NADPH and FAD binding grooves is short (like FNR), while in NOX2 and DUOX1 it is longer, suggesting that activation requires an internal rearrangement within the DH that brings the NADPH groove closer to the FAD site rather than global domain repositioning.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated 'It rather appears that the NADPH-binding conformation is pivotal to enzyme activation,' which directly supports the authors' hypothesis about internal DH rearrangement being critical for activation. This mechanistic insight was viewed as a major contribution of the work.

result: SpNOX appears to be a good model of an activated form of NOX2, which was subsequently confirmed by a CryoEM structure of activated neutrophil NADPH oxidase (Liu et al., 2024) showing relative movement of the NBD towards the FBD subdomain allowing productive NADPH binding.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated 'the manuscript nicely shows that the domain rotations are unlikely to be the main mechanistic element of NOX regulation. It rather appears that the NADPH-binding conformation is pivotal to enzyme activation,' supporting the model. The subsequent publication of activated NOX2 structure confirming the authors' hypothesis further validates this conclusion, though this occurred after the initial review.

result: During review, concurrent CryoEM structures of SpNOX (Dubach et al., 2023) at 2.33-2.75 Å resolution were published, which are essentially the same as the crystal structures presented, validate the anticipated NADPH binding site, confirm the critical roles of K250, S348, and Y353 in NAD(P)H binding, and strongly support the critical role of F397 in tuning the hydride transfer mechanism.
evaluation: The authors acknowledge the concurrent work and demonstrate that both the CryoEM and crystal structures reach the same conclusions, particularly regarding F397's role and NADPH binding. Reviewer 3 noted in the revised version comments that 'the revised version is perfect and represents a major contribution to our understanding of the molecular details of Nox function,' indicating acceptance of how the authors integrated the concurrent findings.
